title: Age effects: Specifications precede displacement conclusions
desc: Outlines subgroup and robustness comparisons for AI employment research without reporting results or establishing entry-level harm.

kps.k: This cluster concerns how to test age-specific AI employment effects, rather than establishing entry-level displacement.
kps.d: The August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? compares employment in the most AI-exposed occupational quintile with quintile 1 by age. It tracks occupation-level long-difference coefficients as the endpoint advances, using a balanced panel of firms observed from January 2018. The supplied excerpts establish this design but do not establish the final observation date or provide readable effect estimates.

kps.k: Age and sex comparisons examine whether employment patterns differ across worker groups, but the excerpts do not report those differences.
kps.d: The appendix compares workers aged 22–25 with groups aged 26–30, 31–34, 35–40 and 41–49, and calculates employment changes by age and exposure separately for men and women. These comparisons address heterogeneity relevant to the entry-level displacement debate; the captions alone do not show which groups experienced larger changes or whether any differences were statistically significant.

kps.k: Specification comparisons provide a framework for assessing alternative explanations, not a demonstrated robustness finding.
kps.d: The figures compare estimates without controls against specifications controlling for interest rates, education, work from home and all three together. The supplied material does not reveal whether estimates change across specifications. A detached table fragment gives occupation counts and significance thresholds without interpretable coefficients. No substantive disagreement can be resolved from these excerpts: readers need the underlying estimates and identification argument before using this revision to support causal displacement claims or workforce decisions, including claims about junior legal employment.

vlens.an: The academia-and-research source supports the proposition that the supplied material establishes methods for testing age-specific AI employment effects but does not establish entry-level displacement. It documents comparisons between the most and least exposed occupational quintiles by age, alongside alternative control specifications and separate calculations for men and women. At the same time, the excerpts provide no readable effect estimates, substantive subgroup findings or evidence that results are robust across specifications. Because this professional voice contains only one source, the record does not support claims about broader prevalence or material internal variation within academia and research.

elens.an: The August 2026 source supports the proposition by documenting an empirical framework for testing age-specific AI employment effects rather than, in the supplied excerpts, establishing entry-level displacement. It compares the most AI-exposed occupational quintile with the least exposed across age groups, advances the endpoint of occupation-level long differences over time, and examines alternative control specifications. It also extends the heterogeneity analysis by calculating age-and-exposure patterns separately for men and women. Material variation lies in the dimensions tested—age bands, sex, exposure quintiles and controls—not in competing substantive conclusions: the excerpts provide no readable effect estimates, robustness results or causal identification sufficient to infer that younger workers, including junior legal workers, have been displaced. Because this time period contains only one curated source, no cross-source variation can be assessed, and its inclusion should not be treated as evidence of broader prevalence.
